{"timeline":[{"headline":"Discovery and Development","text":"Lamotrigine was discovered in the 1980s by researchers at the pharmaceutical company Burroughs Wellcome (now part of GlaxoSmithKline).","date":"1980"},{"headline":"FDA Approval for Epilepsy","text":"Lamotrigine was approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the treatment of epilepsy in 1994.","date":"1994"},{"headline":"FDA Approval for Bipolar Disorder","text":"In 2003, the FDA approved lamotrigine for the maintenance treatment of bipolar I disorder to delay the time to occurrence of mood episodes (depression, mania, hypomania, mixed episodes) in adults treated for acute mood episodes with standard therapy.","date":"2003"}]}

{"timeline":[{"headline":"First Concept of Internal Combustion Engine","text":"In 1680, Dutch physicist Christiaan Huygens designed an internal combustion engine fueled by gunpowder, but it was never built.","date":"1680"},{"headline":"First Working Internal Combustion Engine","text":"In 1807, Swiss engineer François Isaac de Rivaz built the first internal combustion engine, which was powered by a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen.","date":"1807"},{"headline":"First Commercial Internal Combustion Engine","text":"In 1859, Belgian engineer Étienne Lenoir developed the first commercially successful internal combustion engine, which ran on coal gas.","date":"1859"},{"headline":"Four-Stroke Engine Cycle Invented","text":"In 1861, Alphonse Beau de Rochas patented the four-stroke engine cycle, which later became the basis for modern internal combustion engines.","date":"1861"},{"headline":"First Four-Stroke Engine Built","text":"In 1876, Nikolaus Otto built the first practical four-stroke internal combustion engine, known as the Otto engine.","date":"1876"},{"headline":"First Two-Stroke Engine Developed","text":"In 1879, Karl Benz developed the first two-stroke internal combustion engine.","date":"1879"},{"headline":"First Gasoline-Powered Automobile","text":"In 1885, Karl Benz built the first automobile powered by an internal combustion engine fueled by gasoline.","date":"1885"},{"headline":"Diesel Engine Invented","text":"In 1893, Rudolf Diesel developed the diesel engine, which used compression ignition rather than spark ignition.","date":"1893"},{"headline":"First Mass-Produced Car with Internal Combustion Engine","text":"In 1908, the Ford Model T became the first mass-produced car with an internal combustion engine, revolutionizing transportation.","date":"1908"}]}

{"timeline":[{"headline":"Early Ketchup Recipes","text":"The earliest known recipes for ketchup date back to the 17th century in China, where it was made from fermented fish brine, herbs, and spices. This sauce was known as 'ke-chiap' or 'kê-tsiap'.","date":"1600"},{"headline":"Introduction to the West","text":"Ketchup was introduced to the Western world in the late 17th century by British sailors who encountered the sauce in Southeast Asia. They brought it back to England, where it was adapted to local tastes.","date":"1690"},{"headline":"Mushroom Ketchup","text":"In the 18th century, ketchup recipes in England began to include mushrooms as a primary ingredient, creating a dark, rich sauce that was popular before the advent of tomato ketchup.","date":"1700"},{"headline":"Tomato Ketchup Emergence","text":"Tomato ketchup began to emerge in the early 19th century in the United States. The first known recipe for tomato-based ketchup appeared in 1812, created by scientist James Mease.","date":"1812"},{"headline":"Commercial Production Begins","text":"The first commercial ketchup was produced by Jonas Yerkes in 1837. He was the first to sell tomato ketchup in bottles, making it widely available to the public.","date":"1837"},{"headline":"Heinz Ketchup Introduction","text":"Henry J. Heinz launched his brand of ketchup in 1876, which became one of the most popular and enduring brands of ketchup worldwide. Heinz's recipe included ripe tomatoes and a unique blend of spices.","date":"1876"},{"headline":"Standardization of Ketchup","text":"By the early 20th century, ketchup had become standardized in its ingredients and production methods, primarily using tomatoes, vinegar, sugar, and spices. This standardization helped solidify its place as a staple condiment.","date":"1900"}]}

{"timeline":[{"headline":"Establishment of Shu Kingdom","text":"The Shu Kingdom was established in the Sichuan Basin during the Zhou Dynasty, marking the early historical period of Sichuan. This kingdom was later conquered by the Qin state.","date":"-1046"},{"headline":"Conquest by Qin","text":"In 316 BCE, the Qin state conquered the Shu and Ba kingdoms, incorporating the Sichuan Basin into its territory. This conquest was crucial for the Qin's eventual unification of China.","date":"-0316"},{"headline":"Three Kingdoms Period","text":"During the Three Kingdoms period (220-280 CE), Sichuan was the heartland of the Shu Han state, one of the three rival states vying for control of China.","date":"0220"},{"headline":"Tang Dynasty Prosperity","text":"Sichuan experienced significant economic and cultural prosperity during the Tang Dynasty (618-907 CE), becoming a major center for trade and agriculture.","date":"0618"},{"headline":"Mongol Invasion","text":"In 1259, the Mongols invaded Sichuan, leading to significant destruction and the eventual incorporation of the region into the Yuan Dynasty.","date":"1259"},{"headline":"Ming Dynasty Rebuilding","text":"During the Ming Dynasty (1368-1644), Sichuan underwent extensive rebuilding and population growth after the devastation of the Mongol invasion.","date":"1368"},{"headline":"Qing Dynasty and Population Growth","text":"The Qing Dynasty (1644-1912) saw a significant increase in Sichuan's population, making it one of the most populous provinces in China.","date":"1644"},{"headline":"Sichuan in the Republic of China","text":"After the fall of the Qing Dynasty, Sichuan became part of the Republic of China in 1912, experiencing political instability and warlordism.","date":"1912"},{"headline":"Sichuan during the Second Sino-Japanese War","text":"During the Second Sino-Japanese War (1937-1945), Sichuan served as a refuge for Chinese civilians and a base for the Nationalist government.","date":"1937"},{"headline":"Establishment of the People's Republic of China","text":"In 1949, the People's Republic of China was established, and Sichuan became a province under the new communist government.","date":"1949"},{"headline":"Sichuan Earthquake","text":"On May 12, 2008, Sichuan was struck by a devastating earthquake, resulting in significant loss of life and property damage.","date":"2008-05-12"}]}

{"timeline":[{"headline":"Invention of Polyethylene Terephthalate","text":"Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) was first synthesized in 1941 by British chemists John Rex Whinfield and James Tennant Dickson, who worked for the Calico Printers' Association in Manchester, England.","date":"1941"},{"headline":"First Commercial Production of PET","text":"The first commercial production of polyethylene terephthalate (PET) began in 1946, following its invention and patenting.","date":"1946"},{"headline":"Introduction of PET Bottles","text":"In 1973, Nathaniel Wyeth patented the first PET bottle, which became a popular choice for packaging due to its lightweight and shatter-resistant properties.","date":"1973"},{"headline":"Recycling of PET","text":"The recycling of PET began in earnest in the 1980s, with the development of processes to recycle PET bottles into new products, reducing waste and promoting sustainability.","date":"1980s"}]}
